analysis.one_liner: Requires rerouting of dangerous chemical rail shipments around major cities, with whistleblower protection for rail workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Homeland Security Department to write rules for rail shipments of extremely hazardous chemicals, including rerouting them around designated high-threat areas like dense cities and the capital. It would have forced railroads to tell governors, mayors, and local emergency responders what dangerous chemicals move through their communities, protected rail workers who report safety violations from being fired, authorized training grants for workers and first responders, and let cities sue violators for up to $1 million per violation. It was referred to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near rail lines carrying toxic inhalation hazards, flammable gases, explosives, and high-level nuclear waste. The bill's own findings cite estimates that a successful attack on a 90-ton chlorine tanker near a public event on the National Mall could kill or injure up to 100,000 people in under 30 minutes, and notes such shipments are routed through densely populated areas including near the White House and Capitol. It would have benefited rail workers through whistleblower protection and federally funded hazmat training, and local governments through mandatory disclosure of what chemicals pass through their jurisdictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents and workers near hazardous rail lines

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Homeland Security Secretary to issue regulations requiring rail shipments of extremely hazardous materials to be rerouted around designated high-threat corridors, with narrow exceptions for shipments originating or ending there, when no practical alternate route exists, or in emergencies.

Requires railroads to notify governors, mayors, and local emergency responders in high-threat corridors of the quantity and type of extremely hazardous materials shipped through their area, with annual reports and quarterly updates on significant changes.

Prohibits railroads from firing or discriminating against employees who report possible violations of the act to federal authorities, and lets affected workers sue in federal court for reinstatement and compensatory damages.

Authorizes $100 million in grants for hazmat safety training and equipment for rail workers, responders, and repair crews, plus $10 million per year for a new Railway Hazmat Training Program run through nonprofit employee organizations.
Lets any state or local government sue rail shippers for up to $1 million per violation, and authorizes administrative penalties of up to $1 million for each failure to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Railroad owners and operators and chemical shippers, who would bear the cost of rerouting shipments around high-threat corridors (a longer haul means higher operating expense, per the bill's own findings), compliance with disclosure and reporting requirements, and exposure to $1 million penalties and lawsuits. Some of those costs could be passed to chemical customers and their consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself concedes the principal cost of rerouting is additional operating expense from longer hauls; those costs would fall on railroads and shippers and could be passed through to consumers of chemicals and products made from them.

Whistleblower protections apply only to disclosures about violations of this act, not to broader safety complaints, and employees who participate in a violation or knowingly give false information are excluded.

The re-routing mandate includes an exception system left largely to the Secretary's discretion, and the bill's deadline structure — regulations due 90 days after enactment — was aggressive enough that it built in default lists of corridors and materials if the review was not finished in time, which could have produced rushed rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's centerpiece — rerouting toxic and explosive shipments away from dense population centers — trades a modest, quantifiable cost (extra miles hauled, on less than 5% of rail hazmat shipments, per the bill's findings) against reducing exposure to a low-probability but potentially catastrophic attack or accident. The disclosure, whistleblower, and training provisions are low-cost and directly protective. The main design weakness is that much is left to the Secretary's discretion, including the exception process and corridor designations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Homeland Security and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, then sent to subcommittees, and died there when the Congress ended, never reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. David Obey introduced the bill on July 28, 2005, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to both the Homeland Security Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced.
Within two days it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads and the Subcommittee on Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads and chemical shippers avoided rerouting mandates, $1 million penalties, and lawsuits; communities near hazardous rail lines got no new disclosure or rerouting requirements.

for.name: Rep. David Obey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case in its findings that toxic rail shipments near dense population areas posed a catastrophic risk needing rerouting, disclosure, and penalties.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to the Subcommittee on Railroads, and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Homeland Security Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to the Subcommittee on Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed rerouting requirements around high-threat corridors, mandatory chemical disclosure to local officials, whistleblower liability, and up to $1 million penalties per violation plus state and local lawsuits. Its death left railroads free to route toxic shipments through dense areas without disclosure.

Shippers of toxic-by-inhalation gases, explosives, and anhydrous ammonia would have faced rerouting costs from longer hauls and electronic tracking requirements. Because the bill never advanced, current routing practices continued unchanged.

industries.industry: Rail hazmat workers and their unions
industries.note: The bill offered whistleblower protection for workers reporting violations and funded training grants routed partly to national nonprofit employee organizations. Workers gained nothing because the bill died.
